# Enhancing Chat Language Models by Scaling High-quality Instructional Conversations
- **Core Insight:** A 1,468,352-dialogue multi-turn instruction corpus can be generated with no human-written queries by driving two separate ChatGPT Turbo APIs — one prompted as the user, one as the assistant — over a hand-built three-sector taxonomy; the result averages 3.8 turns and 1467.4 tokens per dialogue, the highest of the eight datasets compared (Table 5).
- **Guideline:** When synthesizing dialogue data without human seeds, generate the opening lines from an enumerated taxonomy and give the user-side model an explicit role prompt at every turn, because with dialogue history alone the user model drifts into assistant behavior (§4.4).
- **Authors:** Ning Ding, Yulin Chen, Bokai Xu, Yujia Qin, Zhi Zheng, Shengding Hu, et al. (Tsinghua University)
- **Year:** 2023 (arXiv v1 2023-05; EMNLP 2023)
- **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14233
- **Source type:** paper; the construction details are extended by the official repository https://github.com/thunlp/UltraChat
- **Relevant topics:** synthetic dialogue data, multi-turn chat, taxonomy-driven generation, user simulation, instruction tuning

## Abstract
The paper argues that scaling the diversity and quality of instruction data improves chat models, and releases UltraChat, a systematically designed instructional-conversation dataset that contains no human queries. Coverage is organized as three sectors rather than as task types, so the corpus is meant to span the breadth of interactions a user might have with an assistant. Two separate ChatGPT Turbo APIs are called iteratively, one producing the user turn and one the assistant turn. The released corpus holds 1.5 million multi-turn dialogues. A statistical comparison against seven other instruction datasets reports UltraChat highest on scale, average turns, average length, and lexical diversity. A LLaMA-13B model fine-tuned on UltraChat, called UltraLLaMA, scores 9.023 ± 0.952 on a ChatGPT-judged 300-question set, above Vicuna at 8.961 ± 0.718 (Table 1).

## Key Contributions
- A dialogue-synthesis protocol in which both sides are model-generated and the opening lines come from an enumerated taxonomy rather than from scraped prompts (§3.1, §4).
- Three sectors defined by the kind of information work rather than by task: Questions about the World, Creation and Generation, and Assistance on Existing Materials (§3.1).
- A user-simulation procedure that re-states the user role and the dialogue's purpose at each turn, plus removal of filler politeness from user turns (§4.4).
- A statistical comparison of eight instruction datasets on scale, turns, length, lexical diversity, topic diversity, and ChatGPT-judged coherence (Table 5).
- UltraLLaMA, a LLaMA-13B model trained on the corpus, with its evaluation against seven open baselines (§4.6, §5).

## Key Figures/Tables to Study
- Figure 1 — the construction diagram; the "3~7 rounds of generation" annotation appears on the Sector I panel.
- Table 2 — the 30 meta-concepts used for Sector I.
- Table 3 — the 20 text-material types used for Sectors II and III.
- Table 4 — the seven manually designed templates that concatenate a C4 passage with a generated instruction.
- Table 5 — the dataset statistics comparison, including the topic-diversity column where UltraChat is not best.
- Table 1 — UltraLLaMA against seven open baselines under ChatGPT judging.

## Technical Details
### Generation loop
Two separate ChatGPT Turbo APIs are used, one generating the user query and one the response, called iteratively (§1). The paper does not name a model snapshot beyond "ChatGPT Turbo APIs".

### Sector I — Questions about the World (§4.1)
- ChatGPT generates 30 comprehensive topics covering aspects of daily life (Table 2).
- Each topic is expanded into 30 to 50 subtopics or related concepts.
- 10 questions are generated per subtopic, and ChatGPT is then asked for 10 further questions based on each original question.
- A second branch uses Wikidata entities refined by frequency in Wikipedia articles, keeping the 10,000 most frequent. Per entity: 5 meta-questions, then 10 more specific questions and 20 extended questions.
- Approximately 500,000 questions are filtered and sampled as opening lines.
- The repository states the derived subtopic count as "1100+" and the sampling as 200k specific + 250k general + 50k meta-questions, each rolled out as a 3~7-round dialogue (GitHub README, "Questions about the World"). The paper gives the 30-to-50 expansion rule but not the total.

### Sector II — Creation and Generation (§4.2)
- Text materials are categorized into 20 types (Table 3); ChatGPT produces a range of instructions for each type.
- Approximately 80% of the generated instructions are fed back to ChatGPT to produce more detailed instructions.
- These instructions serve as opening lines. Throughout generation the user prompt re-states the objective, which is to generate and refine a piece of writing.
- The repository adds the per-type count, 200 instructions per writing type, and a 2~4-round dialogue per instruction (GitHub README, "Writing and Creation"). Neither number is in the paper.

### Sector III — Assistance on Existing Materials (§4.3)
- Passages come from the C4 corpus. Each C4 piece carries a source URL; keywords are hand-curated for each of the 20 material types and matched against the URL to classify the text.
- Up to 5 distinct instructions are generated per passage, then combined with the passage using one of seven manual templates (Table 4).
- The paper states two counts that do not reconcile: "we collect 10,000 text pieces from the C4 corpus" and "the concatenated set of 500,000 pieces serves as the opening lines" (§4.3). With 5 instructions per passage, 500,000 openings implies 100,000 passages. The repository states "~10w" (100,000) materials from C4 (GitHub README, "Assistance on Existent Materials"), which is consistent with the 500,000 figure. Treat 10,000 as a probable misprint and cite 500,000 opening lines.

### User simulation and filtering (§4.4)
- Given only the dialogue history, the user model tends to adopt the assistant role. The fix is to include prompts that explicitly assign user personalities, and in Sector II a prompt that restates the dialogue's purpose.
- After generation, "a further filtration step is performed to ensure overall data quality". No threshold, classifier, or rejection rate is published.
- Excessively polite user statements — "Thank you", "Thanks", "You're welcome" — are explicitly excluded from subsequent model output.

### Reported corpus statistics (Table 5)
- UltraChat: 1,468,352 dialogues; 3.8 average turns; 1467.4 average tokens per dialogue; 309.3 average tokens per utterance; lexical diversity (MTLD) 74.3; topic diversity 0.702; ChatGPT coherence 9.06; user simulation yes.
- Comparison points in the same table: SODA 1,486,869 dialogues at 3.6 turns and 231.8 tokens; Baize 210,311 at 3.1 turns and 293.9 tokens, coherence 9.06; GPT4ALL 711,126 single-turn, topic diversity 0.692.
- Topic diversity is a lower-is-better cosine-distance measure over 10,000 sampled dialogues; UltraChat (0.702) is behind GPT4ALL (0.692) and the paper attributes this to the large token count per instance regularizing the embeddings (§4.5).

## Findings relevant to generality and long context
- Coverage is decided entirely by the taxonomy: the paper's stated principle is to avoid task-typed construction and instead span three sectors of information work (§3.1). What the 30 meta-concepts and 20 material types omit is structurally absent from the corpus.
- Breadth is measured only by lexical and topic diversity over 10,000 samples and by a 300-question ChatGPT-judged set plus the Vicuna benchmark (§4.5, §5). There is no held-out task suite and no contamination check.
- Length, not turn depth, is where UltraChat leads: 3.8 average turns against SODA's 3.6 and Baize's 3.1, but 1467.4 tokens per dialogue against 231.8 and 293.9 (Table 5). The paper reports no measure of how often a later turn depends on an earlier one, so the corpus cannot be used as evidence about long-range dialogue dependency.
- The realism control is negative-only: filler politeness is removed and user personalities are prompted (§4.4). No user-realism measurement is reported.

- Checked on 2026-09-18 against: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14233 (v1 PDF, 2023-05-23) and https://github.com/thunlp/UltraChat (README as served 2026-09-18)
- Corrections to the previous card version:
  - Title "UltraChat Pipeline: Scalable Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Generation" → the published title "Enhancing Chat Language Models by Scaling High-quality Instructional Conversations". The file name is unchanged because other pages link `[[ultrachat-pipeline]]`.
  - Sector II named "Writing and Creation" → §3.1 and §4.2 name it "Creation and Generation"; the Figure 1 panel label is "Creation and Writing", and the repository uses "Writing and Creation".
  - "Expands them into 1100+ subtopics" → the paper states 30 to 50 subtopics per meta-topic (§4.1); "1100+" is a repository figure, now attributed there.
  - "For each type, generates 200 instructions" → not in the paper; attributed to the repository.
  - "extracts about ~100k diverse materials from C4" → the paper states 10,000 text pieces and 500,000 concatenated opening lines in the same paragraph (§4.3); both are now given with the repository's "~10w" reading noted.
  - "1.5 million multi-turn dialogues" as the corpus size → 1.5 million is the abstract's rounding; Table 5 gives 1,468,352.
  - "UltraLM" → the paper names the trained model UltraLLaMA (§4.6).
  - Missing **Source type**, corpus statistics, and UltraLLaMA training settings added.
- Removed as unsupported by the source:
  - "public preview shows list lengths from 4 to 14" and the `id` / `data` record schema. These describe a Hugging Face dataset preview, not the paper, and the card's stated URL is the arXiv page.
  - "It is an early clean example of taxonomy-first synthetic data design", "it helped establish synthetic multi-turn dialogue as a practical substitute for scarce human-authored chat transcripts", and the "Why UltraChat matters technically" list. Claims about the field's later practice, not results in this paper.
  - "more informative as a generation-protocol reference than as a fully transparent filtering recipe" — replaced by the paper's own statement that a filtration step exists with no published thresholds (§4.4).
- Not reported by the source: the ChatGPT snapshot used for generation; the rejection rate or criteria of the filtration step; the per-sector dialogue counts; the fraction of turns that depend on earlier turns; UltraLLaMA's learning rate, epochs, and optimizer.
